newsitem.title: USA: Dollar closes lower in U.S., battered by Rubin.
newsitem.headline: Dollar closes lower in U.S., battered by Rubin.

text.p: The dollar sank in afternoon U.S. trade, ending sharply lower after comments from Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin sparked a furious dollar selloff.
Rubin surprised currency players by telling reporters he was looking forward to discussing the dollar's recent rally at a meeting of global finance officials in Berlin on Saturday.

By acknowledging the concerns of his counterparts from other nations in the Group of Seven industrialized powers--notably Japan--Rubin seemed to depart from his singular devotion to a strong dollar, triggering waves of dollar selling, dealers said.

"This is the first time Rubin has mentioned the excessive weakness of the Japanese yen. It was a considerable degradation of the stance of U.S. monetary authorities," said Keisuke Aso, manager of corporate foreign exchange at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
Rubin's comments to reporters in Washington raised expectations that the G7 would make a formal statement at the conclusion of its meeting that would call for a halt to the dollar's meteoric rise.
The greenback finished at 1.6605/15 marks, down from 1.6670/75 at the open, and 123.08/18 yen, down from 124.20/25.
The dollar traded as low as 121.40 yen and 1.6510 marks after the Rubin comments.
Before Friday's losses, the dollar in 1997 had risen 8.7 percent on the mark and 7.5 percent versus the yen. But Rubin frightened many late-arriving dollar bulls, dealers said.
"We saw a massive exodus out of long dollar positions on the Rubin comments. It was very bloody," said Jay Wertheimer, senior foreign exchange trader at Banco di Sicilia.
Rubin appeared to contradict German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who was quoted in a German newspaper early on Friday saying he saw no point in setting exchange rate targets.
Traders read Waigel's words as a rebuttal to persistent calls from Japanese officials to slow the dollar's advance.

"Some people were not certain, given the comments from Waigel, that the G7 nations were in sync. After Rubin's comment, it appears the Japanese and the Americans may be thinking the dollar has gone up enough," said Stephen Jury, chief foreign exchange dealer at Union Bank of Switzerland.
Waigel's words helped push the dollar to a fresh four-year high at 124.72 yen and a 32-month peak at 1.6755 marks.
The dollar also benefited from a report showing solid job growth in the United States with very little wage inflation.
While nonfarm payrolls rose by a surprisingly large 271,000 in January, average hourly earnings were nearly flat, encouraging dollar bulls.

U.S. stocks and bonds also surged on the news, helping pull the dollar higher as well. The Dow Jones industrials ended 82.74 points higher at 6855.80 and the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond rose 22/32.
"All the news that we have been getting lately has been bullish for U.S. asset markets and that has added to dollar bullishness," said Anjum Sayyed, currency trader at Manufacturers and Traders Bank.
The dollar also endured volatile swings versus the Swiss franc, climbing to 1.4460 francs before sinking to 1.4290/00, down from 1.4405/15 at the open.
The British pound rose to $1.6300/07 from $1.6288/95. The dollar ended little changed at Canadian $1.3502/07 versus C$1.3509/14.
The Australian dollar edged higher to $0.7617/22 from $0.7614/19 at the open.
